result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.get_average_degree()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Calculate average degree across all nodes. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L36871-L36927){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.get_average_degree() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Average degree](/assets/graphs/get-average-degree.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A five-node undirected graph with each node's degree in a badge: A 2, B 3, C 3, D 3, E 1. The card adds the degrees to 12, divides by 5 nodes, and gives the average degree 2.4." width="100%"} For directed graphs, this returns the average of (in-degree + out-degree). For undirected graphs, each edge contributes to the degree of both endpoints. In both cases the result equals `2 * edges / nodes`, since every edge adds one to the degree of each of its two endpoints. Average degree is a single-number summary of how densely connected a network is, which makes it handy for: - comparing the connectivity of networks of different sizes (unlike edge counts) - sanity-checking a generated or imported graph against an expected density - choosing parameters for random-graph models that should match a real network A single average can hide a lot: a five-node star and a five-node path both have an average degree of `1.6` but very different structures. Look at `get_degree_distribution()` for the full picture. Edge weights are ignored, parallel edges each count, and an empty graph gives `0.0`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Mean degree value across all nodes. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~get_agg_degree_total`) : Mean, median, and other degree summaries over chosen nodes. [](`~get_degree_distribution`) : How many nodes have each degree. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Every node in a 4-cycle has exactly two neighbors, so the average degree comes out to exactly `2.0`: ::: {#9a41f1a2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "A")]) ) graph.get_average_degree() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 2.0 ``` ::: ::: A five-node star has four edges, so its average degree is `2 * 4 / 5 = 1.6`, even though the hub has degree `4` and every other node has degree `1`: ::: {#ba78404f .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} ec.Graph().add_star_graph(5).get_average_degree() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 1.6 ``` ::: :::
